summary: Adversarially review the round-7 paper edits (proof fixes, credits, *2/*3 facts) against the evidence files

confirmed.quote: Tablebases of up to four men on the cylinder and the torus confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate, and show that two bishops still can.
confirmed.problem: The new clause 'show that two bishops still can' is false as read: the sentence's subject covers the cylinder and the torus, but two bishops win nothing on the torus. It also drops the 'opposite colors' qualifier on which the cylinder result depends.
confirmed.evidence: sections/10_tablebases.tex Table tab:tb: KBBK is 100% won on the cylinder (mate in 14) but 0 won on the torus ('---'); the table note says 'KBBK has the bishops on opposite colors', and the text says 'On the torus only KRRK and KQRK force mate'. Same-color bishops are not claimed to win anywhere.
confirmed.fix: Restrict the claim: '...confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate on the cylinder, and show that on the cylinder two bishops of opposite colors still can.'

verdict.reason: The defect holds. The abstract sentence reads "Tablebases of up to four men on the cylinder and the torus confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate, and show that two bishops still can." The two verbs share one subject, so "still can" reads as applying to both boards. Table tab:tb in 10_tablebases.tex gives KBBK as 0% won on the torus (Mate "---"), and RESULTS.md says the same ("KBB ... 0% won" on the torus). Section X.A says "On the torus only KRRK and KQRK force mate". So the added clause is false for the torus. Before this round the sentence was true on both boards, because KRK is 2.80% won on the cylinder and 0% on the torus. The edit made it false on one of them. The bishop result is also specific to the cylinder (100% won, mate in 14) and to opposite-colored bishops, which the table note and the section's own heading both state, while the abstract says only "two bishops". The omitted qualifier is a smaller point than the torus overreach, since "two bishops" conventionally means the bishop pair. The body is consistent with the cylinder-only reading: it says the Muller claim is contradicted "there", on the cylinder. Only the abstract's scope is wrong. I found nothing that refutes the finding.
verdict.better_fix: In 00_abstract.tex, replace "confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate, and show that two bishops still can." with "confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate, and show that on the cylinder two bishops of opposite colors still can." This keeps the sentence structure, drops the torus overreach, and adds the qualifier the table note uses. If the abstract needs the length back, "two opposite-colored bishops still can on the cylinder" is equivalent.

confirmed.fix: Add a label that matches the stored evidence (C1, or C2 if B's rerun is saved). State in Sec. 09_real that 'decisive' means end positions of one greedy support and that the kpsolve runs were queen-only, or reword the conclusion as 'the 12 end positions with 8 men in the support we found'.

verdict.reason: The defect is real but small. The count itself is correct. research/star2_oracle/REPORT.md section 4.1 lists 5 decisive 8-man terminals for A and 7 for B (24 sides). kpsolve gives exact values equal to the model on every side, and the 9 to 11 man sides are the ones not run. What fails is how the paper presents it. (1) Nothing in the body supports "twelve". Sec. 09_real.tex (lines 66-72) says only that the oracle values of A and B are open. The 12 appear for the first time in the conclusion, in this round's edit, so a reader cannot trace them. The sentence's only label, \lab{C1}, is attached to the uniqueness claim in the following sentence, not to the twelve. The intro says headline numbers carry labels, and the neighbouring items do (C2 on the 78.94% in item 5). (2) The qualifier the paper uses everywhere else is missing. kpsolve is queen-promotions-only, and Sec. 09_real says so for the 1/8 ("queen promotions only") and the intro says so. Only A's 10 sides have a second check, Searcher plus Lichess tablebase with all promotions (tb_A_8men.json). B's 14 sides are single-program and queen-only (REPORT.md: "B has no second implementation"). The unqualified "agree with the model" therefore overstates B. The combined label should be C1. (3) "Decisive" has no definition for A and B. It is the greedy minimal support of min_support.py, which the report says is "not shown to be smallest or unique". The paper's only gloss is the 1/8 sentence "end positions that decide the value". Two things weaken the finding but do not refute it. Item 1 of the same conclusion already uses "decisive side" and gives no label, and the paper does use "decisive" informally elsewhere (appendix table). The claim is also true as written. So this is an unsupported, unlabeled and unqualified new claim, not a false one.
verdict.better_fix: Make two small edits. (a) In sections/09_real.tex, after "their oracle values are open", add: "For each, a search finds a set of end positions that decide the value, five for A and seven for B with eight men; our king-and-pawn solver (queen promotions only) shows that all twelve agree with the model on both sides \lab{C1}, and the rest have 9 to 11 men." That A and B are the only seven-pawn $\nim{2}$ positions of width at most four rests on one program \lab{C1}." If B's Searcher-plus-tablebase rerun is saved in the repo, B can be upgraded to C2, but the combined label stays C1 until then.

and $\BIG$ exceeds every tempo count, the chess result in Theorem~\ref{thm:validity} is
the outcome class of the $\pm\BIG$ value of the components.
confirmed.problem: The two-line proof of the new corollary invokes Theorem thm:hss, but the corollary's BIG hypothesis does not match that theorem's. The corollary asks that BIG exceed 'every tempo count' (a term never defined; Sec. II says 'any count of spare moves'). Theorem thm:hss needs BIG to exceed 'the number of moves either side can make', which is a larger quantity. As written, the proof does not follow.
confirmed.evidence: sections/05_sums.tex line 103: 'BIG exceeds the number of moves either side can make'. sections/02_rules.tex: 'BIG exceeds any count of spare moves'. The phrase 'tempo count' appears only in the old conjecture text now carried into the corollary.
confirmed.fix: Use the theorem's wording in the corollary: 'and $\BIG$ exceeds the number of moves either side can make'.

verdict.reason: The mismatch is real. The new proof of Corollary cor:v4 (04_kings.tex lines 72-80) says the chess result equals the outcome of W by Theorem thm:validity, and that this equals the outcome of the sum model "by Theorem thm:hss". Theorem thm:hss (05_sums.tex line 103) needs three hypotheses: X is HSS, condition (E) holds, and BIG "exceeds the number of moves either side can make". The corollary supplies HSS and (E) in the same words, but for the third it says "BIG exceeds every tempo count". I grepped all of sections/*.tex. "Tempo count" is never defined; the only other "tempo" hits are informal uses in 12_engines.tex and 14_conclusion.tex. It survives only from the old, unproved conjecture, where loose wording was harmless. Sec. II (02_rules.tex line 31) uses a third phrasing, "any count of spare moves". A count of spare tempo moves reads as a smaller quantity than the total number of moves a side can make. Theorem thm:hss's proof sketch needs the larger bound, because black must run out of moves before white's +BIG does. So the corollary's hypothesis is undefined and does not obviously imply the theorem's, and a two-line proof that invokes the theorem verbatim has a gap at that step. The fix is a single wording change, so severity is low. A refutation would have to show that "tempo count" is defined somewhere or means the theorem's bound, and I found neither.
verdict.better_fix: In 04_kings.tex Corollary cor:v4, replace "and $\BIG$ exceeds every tempo count" with "and $\BIG$ exceeds the number of moves either side can make". This is the wording of Theorem~\ref{thm:hss}, and it removes the undefined term. The rest of the corollary and its proof stay as they are. Optionally, align Sec. II (02_rules.tex line 31, "any count of spare moves") to the same phrase. That line was not edited this round, so the optional change is not needed for this finding.

two $\nim{2}$ positions, A and its mirror
image B, have seven pawns

verdict.better_fix:
Trim to 199 words (whitespace count, same method as before) and scope the bishop claim to the cylinder, by replacing the abstract body with:

Cylinder chess joins the a-file to the h-file, so the board has no edges or corners. We study its king-and-pawn endgames with combinatorial game theory, following Elkies: a passed pawn wins, and the kings are frozen in a mutual zugzwang worth zero. We repair this model with a passed-pawn test that respects en passant, and give conditions under which the frozen kings are exact. Under the new test, an exhaustive census finds no nimber above star with at most six pawns on ordinary boards up to four files wide, but star two appears with seven, in one position and its color-reversed twin, confirmed by three programs; on the three-file cylinder six pawns suffice. We also find positions worth one-eighth, up-second star and Tiny 1, and test them against real chess: with frozen kings and queen promotions only, the one-eighth hinges on one side of one end position. Four-man tablebases on the cylinder and the torus confirm that king and rook can no longer force mate; two bishops still can on the cylinder. We correct earlier work on Dawson's chess on the cylinder: the ring is a first-player win exactly when the strip three files shorter has Grundy value zero.

The word savings come from "worth zero" for "that counts as zero", the shorter repair sentence, "twin" for "mirror image", "positions worth" for "king-and-pawn positions worth", "Four-man tablebases" for "Tablebases of up to four men", and "the ring" for "the full ring". All of the round's content is kept. The existing line breaks can stay or be re-wrapped, since only the word count matters.

confirmed.quote:
is the outcome of the pawn game that ends at the first passed
pawn (the whole-board game $W$ of Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}), without draws.
confirmed.problem: The theorem does not say which pawns W is played on. The Corollary needs W to be exactly the game that Theorem hss compares with S(X), where X is the pawn components. The king group Z contains pawns of its own (line 50), and every move of those pawns is a Z-move that (V3) says loses. So the chess result equals W only when W is played on the pawn components alone, with Z (both kings and its pawns) deleted. Section V defines W only for 'a pawn position X', and the label 'whole-board game' suggests all pawns. The Corollary's 'pawn part' and 'the components' are likewise never tied to W.
confirmed.evidence: LOOPY.md Thm 1.14(i): 'the result is the normal-play result of G1 ⊞ ... ⊞ Gk (Z deleted)', and (V4) is stated for 'the pawn components of Y, ... with the king group Z deleted'. The paper's line 50 defines Z as the two kings plus some pawns. If W included Z's pawns, a Z-pawn push would be a non-losing move in W, contradicting (V3). The audit table (notes/proof_audit2/REPORT.md, Thm 3 row) asked for 'whole-board game W' to be tied to the components. The intro bullet (01_intro.tex line 39, 'whole-board pawn game') inherits the same ambiguity.
confirmed.fix: Write: 'is the outcome of W(X) (Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}), where X is the set of pawn components with the king group Z, its pawns included, deleted, without draws.' In the Corollary, say '(V4) the pawn part X, the components with Z deleted, is hereditarily sum-safe ...' so the chain Theorem validity -> W(X) -> Theorem hss -> S(X) is literally the same X.

verdict.reason: Real but modest: a missing argument, not a false claim under the natural reading. Section V (05_sums.tex line 92) defines W only as W(X) for a pawn position X, and Theorem validity (04_kings.tex lines 62-63) cites "the whole-board game W" with no X. The Corollary proof then chains "chess result = outcome of W" with "Theorem hss: outcome of W = outcome of S" for "the pawn part", with no step saying these are the same X. The text does separate the objects. Line 50 sets "pawn components" apart from Z, and the proof sketch says both sides play the pawn game once Z-moves are excluded as losing. So the intended X is the components with Z deleted, which is what LOOPY.md Thm 1.14(i) and (V4) say ("Z deleted"). The text never says this, however, and two phrases invite the wrong X. Z is defined as the two kings plus some pawns, and "whole-board" reads as the full board. "The pawn part" in the Corollary could also be read to include Z's pawns. With Z's pawns in W, a Z-pawn push would be an ordinary non-losing W-move, which contradicts (V3), so the theorem would be false under that reading. The round-6 audit asked only to replace "normal-play outcome of the components" with "whole-board game W" (notes/proof_audit2/REPORT.md, Thm 3 row). It did not ask for the X to be pinned down. The intro phrase "whole-board pawn game" (01_intro.tex line 39) is only loosely tied to this and needs no change if the theorem is fixed. This is a precision defect, not a proof error, and the repository proof is unaffected.
verdict.better_fix: Name X once, in the theorem and again in the Corollary, so the chain is literally the same X. In the theorem, replace "is the outcome of the pawn game that ends at the first passed pawn (the whole-board game $W$ of Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}), without draws" with: "is the outcome of $W(X)$ (Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}), without draws, where $X$ is the position of the pawn components, with the king group $Z$ and its pawns deleted." In the Corollary, replace "the pawn part" with "the pawn part $X$, the components with $Z$ deleted,". Replace the Corollary proof with: "By Theorem~\ref{thm:validity} the chess result is the outcome of $W(X)$, and by Theorem~\ref{thm:hss} this is the outcome of $S(X)$, the sum model of the components." Optionally change "the whole-board pawn game" in the intro bullet to "the pawn game of the components".

confirmed.quote:
so strips separated by
empty files never interact, and the position after it looks the same to either player, so the game is impartial.
confirmed.problem: The sentence is unqualified, but strip independence and impartiality hold only for the game in which a whole forced sequence counts as one move. At the level of single plies, compulsory capture is a global rule, so strips do interact: a pending capture stops a player from moving in another strip. The ply-level game is partizan, because White and Black push different pawns and reach different positions. The same section's closing paragraph says exactly this: 'Valued on its own as a partizan game, the ordinary 3x5 board is *, although g(5)=3 ... a sum of such values would let a player answer in another strip while a capture is pending.' Read together, the two passages contradict each other.
confirmed.evidence: Lines 90-92 of the same file. notes/lemmas.md Thm 5.3 states the claim for 'the macro-move (impartial) model' and Counterexample 5.4 shows that the partizan sum of the strips predicts the winner wrongly in 3 of 36 two-strip boards. The proof audit (Thm 21 row) asked for two sentences: that other strips have no capture during a forced sequence, and that the macro-game is colour-symmetric. The new sentence derives 'never interact' from locality alone and drops the qualification.
confirmed.fix: Rewrite as: 'Each such sequence is forced (its only available captures are on the pushed file's square) and touches only the pushed file and its neighbors. So, counting a whole sequence as one move, strips separated by empty files are independent, and since both players have the same sequences available and the blocked pair left behind is inert for both, this game of sequences is impartial.' The 'warning about sums' then stays consistent.

verdict.reason:
Real but minor, and it is a precision defect rather than a mathematical error. I could not make it a true contradiction, but I could not clear the sentence either.

What cuts against the finding:
- The section already uses "move" for the whole forced sequence. Line 40 says "Let us see what one move does" and then describes five plies. Line 51 says "a move removes a file and its untouched neighbors". The misère paragraph says "a forced sequence ... ends with the player who began it".
- "The position after it" refers to the sequence.
- The warning's "while a capture is pending" can only happen inside a sequence. It describes why the ply-level partizan sum fails, which is consistent with the macro reading.
- The substance is right. notes/lemmas.md Thm 5.3 argues that "during a macro-move the other strips are quiet". Counterexample 5.4 shows 3 of 36 two-strip boards where the partizan sum predicts the winner wrongly, and the Grundy XOR was right on all 36.

What supports the finding:
- Lines 48-50 say "never interact" and "the game is impartial" with no qualifier. For the game as played ply by ply, both statements are false.
- Compulsory capture is a global rule, so a pending capture in one strip does stop a player from moving in another.
- White and Black push different pawns, and mid-sequence only one side has a capture. The paper itself says at line 90 that the 3x5 board is partizan, with value star.
- A reader meets "the game is impartial" about 40 lines before "Valued on its own as a partizan game", with nothing in between saying the unit is the sequence.
- The proof audit asked for two explicit points: other strips have no capture during a sequence, and the macro-game is colour-symmetric. The new sentence compresses both into "forced" and "looks the same".
- "Looks the same" is also loose. After a white push the dead pair stands on c2/c3, and after a black push it stands on c1/c2. These are different positions, both inert.

One clause fixes it: say that a whole sequence counts as one move, and say that the dead pair is inert for either side.
verdict.better_fix:
In /Users/aritro/Downloads/Research/Chessendgames/paper/ieee/sections/11_dawson.tex, lines 48-50, replace the first sentence with:

"Each such sequence is forced and touches only the pushed file and its neighbors. So, counting a whole sequence as one move, strips separated by empty files never interact; both players have the same sequences available, and the blocked pair left behind is dead for either, so this game of sequences is impartial."

The next sentence, "A strip of $n$ untouched files is therefore the octal game ...", then reads on unchanged. The warning paragraph at line 90 stays consistent, because it concerns the ply-level partizan values.

rejected.why: The facts in the finding are right, but they do not make a defect. I read the cached copies of both pages in the scratchpad (dl_hgm/cyl_hgm.html and dl_wiki/cylinder_chess.wiki). The HGM page says only that a single Rook, Bishop or Knight, or two Knights and Bishops in any combination, cannot force mate on the cylinder. It never mentions the torus or the queen. Wikipedia says a king and rook cannot force mate against a lone king on the cylinder. It also says that on the toroidal board mate is impossible with king and queen versus king, citing Gik 1983. So the sentence "That king and rook cannot force mate on the cylinder, nor king and queen on the torus, is known in prose~\cite{WikiCylinder,HGMCylinder}" is fully supported by the group citation. Wikipedia covers both clauses, and HGM independently backs the rook clause. A grouped cite at the end of a compound sentence is ordinary IEEE practice, and the group as a whole supports the sentence. The paper's own Table I (Table~\ref{tab:tb}) agrees: the torus KQK entry is 0% won, and the paper's text never claims that KRK wins everything on the cylinder. The only objection is that HGM is cited for a clause it does not cover, which is taste, not a false or unsupported statement. The Gik point is also not a defect. rejected.quote:
Elkies asked for a
more systematic treatment of en passant~\cite{Elkies1996}
rejected.problem: The sentence slightly overstates the source. Elkies only says what one might hope for in a closing remark, and he names a CGT-style treatment of en passant together with other entailing moves. He does not make a request about the passed-pawn test.
rejected.why:
The wording is faithful to the source, so the finding is taste, not a defect.

I checked Elkies 1996 in the MSRI printed version (the running heads give the printed page numbers). The remark is on printed p. 148 and runs onto p. 149: "one might also hope for a more systematic CGT-style treatment of en passant captures and entailing chess moves... and ask for a class of positions on an N x N board...". It sits in the closing list of open directions, next to questions such as "Does 1/8 exist on the 8x8 board?". In that list, "one might hope for X" is how Elkies poses a wanted result, so "Elkies asked for a more systematic treatment of en passant" is a fair paraphrase. The finding itself concedes that the page and the gist are right.

The paper's sentence does not claim Elkies said anything about the passed-pawn test. It says he wanted a more systematic treatment of en passant, which he did, and then says "we use a stricter test" as the paper's own step. The citation is also correct: the same paper handles en passant only case by case, on printed pp. 139--140.

The proposed fix would not improve anything. "Hoped for" is only a softer synonym for the same claim. Adding `[p.~148]` would also break the paper's citation style, because no other `\cite` in sections/*.tex or main.tex has an optional page argument. The remark also spans pp. 148--149, so a single page number would be slightly off.

rejected.quote:
Thus $G=\nim{2}$ again. The two analyses
match move for move because B is A with the colors reversed and the files mirrored.
rejected.problem: The new sentence makes the whole preceding walk-through of B redundant. It repeats A's analysis under a symmetry. The same holds for the identical A and B columns of Table tab:star2_settings. It also reads as an afterthought that contradicts the framing of A and B as two independent findings (the theorem lists them as separate positions, and the Conclusion speaks of them as two).
rejected.why:
Refuted. The reviewer's mapping is correct, but it does not show a defect. The new sentence is true and agrees with the rest of the paper.

1. Truth check. Reverse the colors (rank r to 9-r) and mirror the files (a<->d, b<->c). A's white a4 b3 d2 d3 become black d5 c6 a7 a6, and A's black a7 b7 c5 become white d2 c2 b4. That is exactly B. The capture histories map too: c2xd3 becomes b7xa6. The move-by-move claim also holds: a4-a5 maps to d5-d4, d3-d4 to a6-a5, b3-b4 to c6-c5, the c5xd4 reply to b4xa5, a7-a5 to d2-d4, b7-b6 to c2-c3, and the reversible a7-a6 and b7-b5 (white replies worth 2 and 3) to d2-d3 and c2-c4 (black replies worth -2 and -3). This is the same operation the paper already uses for the candidate ("turn the board around and swap the colors"). Table tab:star2_settings shows identical A and B columns in every setting, as symmetry predicts.

2. "Contradicts the framing of A and B as two independent findings." The paper does not frame them that way. In the same round, the abstract (00_abstract.tex line 7) was changed from "in two positions" to "in one position and its color-reversed mirror image". The Counts paragraph now says "A and its mirror image B". The new sentence in Section VIII is what makes these three places agree.

3. The theorem still has to name both placements, because the census is explicitly "without reduction by symmetry or translation". The count of two (A and B, a pair), the engine and solver agreement "on each", and the separate table columns all follow from that. The Conclusion's "Positions A and B" is likewise consistent. Neither the theorem nor the Conclusion claims independence.

4. Redundancy is taste, not a false statement, a logical gap or a broken reference. The two-line sentence tells the reader why the two walk-throughs run in parallel. The proposed fix would delete the only written verification of B and could look like a loss of evidence for a claim backed by a separate solver run. Merging the table columns would hide that the symmetric pair was checked separately.

Nothing here is wrong or unsupported, so I would leave the text as it is.

rejected.quote: a race is won as the race rule says
rejected.problem: The paper has three race rules (count, mover, opponent) and says none is exact chess. 'The race rule' in a theorem hypothesis does not say which one. In the conclusion, $W$ also appears bare in the theorem and its proof, although Section V-C defines the function $W(X)$.
rejected.why:
Not a defect; at most a taste preference.

"The race rule" in (V2): the paper already uses this phrase for whichever rule the model is run under. Examples are sections/06_atlas.tex:61 ("depend on the race rule ($3/4$ becomes $0$ under the mover rule)") and 07_targets.tex:80 ("every race rule"). The repository's LOOPY.md does the same. Section II-D says "Every value uses the default setting, the count rule with the e.p.-aware test, unless we say otherwise", so the default is fixed. The theorem is parametric on purpose. It says that whichever race rule the model (and so W) uses, chess must agree on who wins a race. This is the right hypothesis, and it is what the paper's own failure count says ("34 because a passed pawn does not win its race"). The statement "None is exact chess" in Section II-C does not conflict with it. That sentence says no rule is exact in general. V2 only requires agreement in the positions the theorem covers. The old (V2) said nothing about races, so the new wording closes a gap. Nothing in the text is false, unsupported or contradicted.

Bare $W$: the theorem says "the whole-board game $W$ of Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss}", which names the game outright. The theorem and the corollary have no named pawn part $X$, so $W(X)$ would need a new symbol. The argument of $W$ can only be the pawn part of the position, so there is no ambiguity. In the corollary proof, Theorem~\ref{thm:hss} is cited right beside $W$ and states the identification $S(X)$ versus $W(X)$. Dropping the argument is a harmless abbreviation and does not mislead.

The proposed fix would be a one-word clarification at most ("the model's race rule"). It does not repair any false or missing statement, so I would not make it a reported defect.

rejected.quote: On a board with room for two files beyond the buffer, for every king group
rejected.problem: The added width condition is ambiguous and undefined. It does not say whether the two files lie on one side or on both sides of the buffer, or whether they must be free of the king group, or what 'room' means when the board is a cylinder. The condition is the only thing the edit adds to the conjecture, so the reader cannot tell when it applies.
rejected.why: The wording has a determinate reading, and it matches the derivation behind it. The buffer is defined at 04_kings.tex:50-51 as the neighboring files of the block, so "beyond the buffer" means outside the king group's block and its buffer. The width condition comes from kings/theory/LOOPY.md, Prop 2.10(b) (lines 48 and 756). That entry says the counterexample "requires board width >= |F_Z| + 4", which is the block, a buffer file on each side, and two further files. Its example puts a white pawn on file f and black pawns on f and f+1, so it uses two adjacent context files. LOOPY.md line 551 shows the same layout: on 7x6 with F_Z={a,b,c}, the buffer is {d,g} and the context lies on {e,f}. "Room for two files beyond the buffer" is a faithful paraphrase of that layout. It also handles the cases the reviewer asks about. On a cylinder the buffer has two files. For a group at the edge of an ordinary board the buffer has one, so the paper's wording is slightly sharper than "|F_Z|+4". "Room" for two files reads as a two-file strip, not two scattered files. The reviewer's analogy to the rank count in horizon1 is a fair stylistic wish, but a missing count in a conjecture's hypothesis is taste, not a false or unsupported statement. The proposed fix is worse than the text. "At least two files in neither the king group nor its buffer" permits one file on each side, for example F_Z={c,d} on a six-file ordinary board, where no counter-promotion context exists. That would make the hypothesis wrong in a corner case.

rejected.quote:
and the position after it looks the same to either player, so the game is
impartial
rejected.problem: This is the justification for the impartiality claim, and it is vague. 'Looks the same to either player' does not say what is the same. The step that matters is that a push by black yields the same strip structure with the colors swapped and white to move, so both players have identical moves in every strip. The sentence also calls each sequence 'forced', although the example above it offers a choice of captures ('say b3xc2', 'say d1xc2'). Only the resulting position is forced.
rejected.why: I could not support this as a defect; it is a preference for a longer argument. (1) 'Forced' matches the paper's own usage. The text above the sentence says 'black must capture, say b3×c2', so the choice among equivalent captures is already visible. The theorem says 'every first move with its forced captures', and the misère paragraph says 'A forced sequence has odd length'. The sequence is forced in the chess sense that each ply must be a capture. I replayed all four capture orders: b3xc2 or d3xc2 first, then b1xc2 or d1xc2. Every order ends in the same position, with b and d empty, c2 and c3 blocked, and the opponent to move. Nothing in the sentence claims the individual captures are unique, and no other capture exists on the board to compete with them. (2) 'The position after it looks the same to either player' is terse but correct. By colour symmetry a black push (c3-c2) gives the same strips of untouched files, a dead blocked file with the colours swapped, and white to move. That is the reading the sentence needs, and the paper makes the same colour-symmetry move elsewhere ('By rotation all first moves are alike'). I also checked the other clauses. 'Touches only the pushed file and its neighbors' holds for the five-ply, three-ply and one-ply cases. 'Strips separated by empty files never interact' holds, because the strips are bounded by the emptied b and d files. A blocked file never sits next to an untouched file, because a push consumes untouched neighbors. The sentence also agrees with the 'warning about sums' paragraph, which concerns the ply-level partizan value, not the macro-move game. The reviewer's version would be marginally more explicit, but the current wording is not false, unsupported or a style break.
